dharana.numbering_edition: Jaideva Singh 1979 (dhāraṇā 1 = verse 24; dhāraṇā 82 = verses 105–106 and dhāraṇā 89 = verses 113–114, otherwise one verse each; dhāraṇā 112 = verse 137)
dharana.sanskrit_iast: kvacid vastuni vinyasya śanair dṛṣṭiṃ nivartayet | taj jñānaṃ cittasahitaṃ devi śūnyālayo bhavet ||
dharana.sanskrit_source: GRETIL e-text, compared with Wallis's concordance, Pradīpaka and the Singh scan
sanskrit_variants: verse 120: GRETIL (and Pradīpaka) read śūnyālāyo; corrected to śūnyālayo with Wallis.
dharana.rendering: Having placed the gaze on some object, let one slowly withdraw it, and with it the knowledge of the object, together with the mind; O Goddess, one becomes a dwelling of the void.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: the knowledge and impression of the object can be eliminated either through contemplating the world as void (śūnya-bhāvanā) or through the bhairavī mudrā, eyes open without blinking but attention turned to the Self; either way the external world loses its hold. He classes it as śāktopāya. Wallis: 'yogic withdrawal': fix the gaze, slowly withdraw it, then the thought of it, then the heart-mind itself.
dharana.technique_name: Placing the Gaze, Then Withdrawing It
dharana.instruction: Rest the gaze on one object, then slowly withdraw the gaze, the thought of the object and the mind into emptiness.

checked_against: The Mystery Within (2019), Session Two list: 'Dharana 95' = verse 120 (agrees with Singh)
Wallis concordance: verse 120 = 'Yogic withdrawal (Y95 ~ A3)' (verse text and technique match)
GRETIL, Wallis and Pradīpaka: Sanskrit of verse 120 compared
verification.notes: Door index = Singh dhāraṇā number, read directly in Singh's own headings and cross-checked against The Mystery Within's Singh-numbered list and Wallis's concordance. Caveat: Singh was read from an OCR scan, not a print copy in hand.

numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 120 'Dharana 97', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 95. Not followed.

source_disagreements: Singh's commentary gives an unblinking open-eyed gaze (bhairavī mudrā) as one way to eliminate the object; this is not in the verse and is not taught here.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 120 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

points: the gaze, the knowledge and the mind slowly withdrawn
geometry.summary: Not a body shape. The map is the gaze going out to one object and slowly returning, bringing the knowing of the object back with it into emptiness.
geometry.svg_hint: a dotted line from an eye to a small object, retracting step by step into an open space
geometry.honesty: Geometry records the dharana's own map of attention, not a body shape. Locations marked 'commentarial' come from commentary, not from the verse.

reaction.name: Withdraw slowly
reaction.summary: School metaphor only: attention placed on an object is drawn back slowly, along with the thought of it, until only open space remains. Not a biochemical or medical claim.

breath.lands_in: wherever the breath naturally ends; this door places nothing on the breath
breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

orientation.cue: Place the gaze on one object, then withdraw it slowly
orientation.gravity: Let the floor or chair carry the body completely; there is no posture to hold
orientation.gaze: Eyes open, then softening or closing
orientation.degrees_hint: No angle target: the VBT gives no posture for this dharana

attention.primary: The gaze resting on one simple object
attention.secondary: The slow withdrawal of the gaze, then of the thought of the object, then of the mind, into emptiness

adiyogi.verse_paraphrase: Having placed the gaze on some object, let one slowly withdraw it, and with it the knowledge of the object, together with the mind; O Goddess, one becomes a dwelling of the void.
adiyogi.method_summary: Rest your gaze on one simple object. Then, slowly, withdraw it: let the eyes soften or close, let the thought of the object fade, and let the mind itself settle back, until only open emptiness remains. Rest there.

honesty.disclosure: Door 095 follows Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 95 (verse 120) in Jaideva Singh's numbering. The door-to-dharana index is a School of 112 Doorways teaching device. Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.
honesty.notes: pairing_type is school_device: the dharana is the content, while the door index, seat and pacing are the school's.
flags: Door index = Jaideva Singh dharana number: Door 095 is dharana 95, verse 120. Other editions number differently (see dharana.numbering_variants).
The seat, breath counts, reaction metaphor, attention-map drawing and beat scripts are school devices, not part of the verse.
The English is a school paraphrase, not a quotation from any translator.
No medical claims. Reaction names are metaphors, not biochemistry.

safety.pain_rule: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.
safety.open_seat_alternate: This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
safety.contraindication_notes: General practice caution only; not medical advice. Blink naturally; Singh's mention of an unblinking gaze (bhairavī mudrā) is not taught here. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.

beats.title: Orientation
beats.script: Sit comfortably with a simple object in front of you. Eyes open, blinking naturally.

beats.title: Breath

beats.title: Attention
beats.script: Rest the gaze on the object. Slowly withdraw it. Let the thought of the object fade. Let the mind settle back. Rest in the space.

beats.title: Reaction cue
